Some interactions are positive: healthy populations can be more economically productive, and

set in train favorable demographic trends that lay a foundation for sustained economic growth.

And economic growth can in turn provide additional resources for investing in health and

protecting the poor from health-related financial distress. The health sector can provide

meaningful and productive work for health workers, including in rural areas where other

employment opportunities are limited. Expenditure by government can also finance public goods

not adequately supplied by the private sector (disease surveillance, vector control of

communicable diseases); reduce inequity (through progressive taxation that is then spent on pro-

poor health needs); and address other market failures. But some interactions between health and
